title: An Academic Librarian Reports on the Impact of APA’s New Electronic References Guidelines
extended_summary:
This paper is not the requested 2024 secondary study titled “Impact of ChatGPT on the Academic Writing Quality of Senior High School Students.” Instead, the provided text is a practitioner-oriented column discussing the effects of the American Psychological Association’s 2007 electronic referencing guideline changes, especially the adoption of Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs), on academic library users and citation practices. The author focuses on the confusion created when students and faculty try to cite electronic journal articles, particularly those accessed through subscription databases that do not clearly display DOIs.

The article does not report an empirical intervention study. Rather, it presents an argument and professional reflection about APA’s revised citation rules and their consequences for library instruction, database use, and citation tools such as RefWorks, EndNote, and Zotero. The author explains that users are now often expected to search beyond the database itself for DOIs, article URLs, or journal homepages, which creates friction in the research and writing process.

The population discussed includes undergraduate students, graduate or doctoral students, faculty, librarians, and writing instructors in higher education. The context is academic library and university research support, with particular emphasis on teaching citation practices in colleges and universities. Although the paper refers to schools and departments that require APA style, it does not present a formal sample, outcome dataset, or experimental comparison.

The main conclusion is that APA’s electronic reference changes were introduced before the scholarly ecosystem was ready to support them consistently. The author argues that the rules create substantial confusion for everyday users, especially undergraduates, and recommends a transitional or stop-gap approach, such as permitting database-name citations when DOIs are unavailable. Overall, the article is a commentary or position piece rather than a study of ChatGPT, academic writing quality, or senior high school students.
